name: Palak Bajpai
place: Jabrella, Bharsaua and two further campuses
deck: Four dense little forests inside school and college gates: 1,025 plants across 2,120 square feet, put in on four days. Another 435 saplings are still held back for the next site.
description: Four dense forests on school and college ground, 1,025 plants across 2,120 square feet, planted on four days, with 435 held back for the next one.

aims.h: A forest inside a school gate
aims.p: None of the four plots is large — four hundred square feet at Jabrella, a thousand at The Good Harvest School. Miyawaki planting is what fits ground that size.

aims.h: Buy for the next site as well
aims.p: Fourteen hundred and sixty plants procured, one thousand and twenty-five in the ground, four hundred and thirty-five held back rather than crowded in.
Two primary schools, a school and a college. The four plots sit where children and students walk past them every day of term.

did: Planted 200 plants across 400 sq ft at Primary School, Jabrella
Planted 150 across 350 sq ft at Basic Vidyalaya, Bharsaua
Planted 500 across 1,000 sq ft at The Good Harvest School
Planted 175 across 370 sq ft at Pt. Lalita Prasad Ramkisha Mahavidyalaya
Ran it as a four-person team — Palak leading, Nisha on labour and materials, Roli on sourcing and plantation, Kshama on plant knowledge and outreach
Reached about a thousand more people through Instagram and WhatsApp
Held back 435 of the 1,460 plants procured for continued planting

holes: The report gives four planting dates and no year, and names no district for any of the four sites.

It names no fellow either. The work is credited to a team of four — Palak Bajpai leading, with Nisha, Roli and Kshama. That the fellowship is hers, and that the four sites are at Unnao in Uttar Pradesh, is confirmed by Swechha and not by the report.
The report records what was planted and where. It sets down no objectives, and nobody’s own words.
The site list and one photograph of a site signboard are the only record of the place names, and the photograph is too damaged in the report to read a spelling from.

February and March is not the planting window the Forest Department and the nurseries recommend, and the wheat harvest took the labour. Both are the team’s own account of why the four days fell where they did.
